text: The applicants' details are set out in the appended table.
The Government were represented by Mr G. Matyushkin, Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were subsequently represented by Mr A. Fedorov, Head of the Office of the Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were subsequently represented by Mr M. Galperin, Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.
On the dates indicated in the appended table, the applicants participated in various political demonstrations.
The applicants were apprehended at the venue of the demonstrations.
The applicants were transferred to various police stations in Moscow or St Petersburg after being apprehended.
Administrative records were drawn up at the police stations in Moscow or St Petersburg to which the applicants were transferred.
The records of the administrative offence were based on the reports and explanations of the police officers who had arrested the applicants.
Some of the applicants were released several hours after being taken to the police station.
Some of the applicants spent the night at the police station.

On the dates stipulated in the appended table, the applicants were convicted under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which concerns a refusal to obey the lawful order of a police officer.
Some of the applicants were ordered to pay fines ranging between 500 Russian roubles (RUB) and RUB 1,000.
Some of the applicants were sentenced to administrative imprisonment for three to fifteen days.
The specific sentences imposed on each applicant are set out in the appended table.

The domestic courts relied on the administrative records, the reports and explanations of the police officers when convicting the applicants under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The domestic courts considered it unlawful that some of the applicants shouted slogans during a public assembly in respect of which no advance notification had been submitted to the authorities.

The domestic courts considered it unlawful that some of the applicants refused to stop participating in a public assembly in respect of which no advance notification had been submitted to the authorities.
For a summary of the relevant domestic law, see Navalnyy v. Russia [GC] (application nos. 29580/12 and 4 others, §§ 46-47, judgment of 15 November 2018).

The domestic legal provisions governing administrative transfer (escorting) and detention are set out in the case of Butkevich v. Russia (application no. 5865/07, §§ 33-36, judgment of 13 February 2018).
